newsitem.title: ITALY: UN warns North Korea crop devastated by drought.
newsitem.headline: UN warns North Korea crop devastated by drought.

text.p: Drought in North Korea has devastated 70 percent of the maize crop and could lead to a worsening of the food situation in the famine-threatened country, United Nations agencies said in a joint statement on Monday.

"The crop is lost. It is absolutely disastrous. It is going to be a major catastrophe that no-one realised because they kept on hoping it would rain tomorrow," Roberto Christen, an adviser with the U.N.'s Rome-based Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), said in the statement.

Christen was part of a U.N.-coordinated mission to North Korea at the end of July to assess the effects of the hermit state's worst drought in more than half a century on a crop already devastated by unprecedented flooding in 1995-96.
Official North Korean media reported over the weekend that 100mm of rain had been recorded on Saturday night, giving hope for next October's crucial harvest.
But Monday's statement said even heavy rainfall would not be enough to reverse the situation.

"The observations made so far suggest that approximately 70 percent of the country maize crop will be lost this year without any chances of recuperation even if it rains very soon," the agencies said.

The statement, which was issued by the U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP) in Rome, said over 60 days without rain had destroyed 1.5 million tons of the maize crop on which North Korea had been relying to feed its already hungry people.
"The drought exacerbates the fragility of the agricultural production system, already weakened by two consecutive years of losses due to flood," the agencies said in the statement.

"It will dramatically reduce the availability of cereals for the period November 1997 to October 1998. And it will seriously worsen the difficult food situation in August and September (this year)," it added.
The statement said rice crops, which were previously less affected, were now also in danger.
"Should the drought continue and less water be available for irrigation, the losses on paddyfields could also reach alarming proportions," it said.
Earlier on Monday FAO economist Ajay Markanday said the agency would lead a mission to North Korea next week to further assess the damage.
International aid agencies this year have stepped up calls for food aid to stave off hunger in the Stalinist state, where they warn famine is imminent, especially among young children.
Some reports have likened the disaster to famines seen in Ethiopia in the 1980s. Monday's statement said the situation could get even worse if the drought persisted.
"The above figures are only estimates which can be significantly aggrevated should the drought continue and reservoirs and other water sources further decline," it said.
The WFP launched a fresh appeal last month for $46 million in food aid for the Stalinist state on top of an earlier request for $95.5 million.
